intro: You don't need a budget to get good at telegram bot api key. You need a map of the free tools, and an honest read on the trade-offs between them. Here's that map — researched, written and fact-checked by the same engine that publishes this blog.

We'll walk through Telegram Bot API, Mastodon API, Bluesky At Protocol, and Choose boring technology first — and finish with the questions people actually ask, so you can check before you buy anything. You shouldn't have to buy anything.

sections.heading: Telegram Bot API
paragraphs: Start with the basics. The Telegram Bot API is free, HTTP-based and needs nothing but a token from @BotFather.

The upshot: Create a bot in one message, then send and receive messages, create channels, and drive webhooks entirely over plain HTTPS. It is the cheapest 'social media' channel a self-publishing site can own, and this blog posts to it when a token is configured.
The links in the sources section go straight to the primary docs.
bullets: Message @BotFather and /newbot to get a token
Optionally set a webhook with setWebhook for incoming events

sections.heading: Mastodon API
paragraphs: First, the thing that actually matters: Mastodon's API is free and fully documented — any instance lets you register an app and post programmatically.

In other words: Create an app in your instance's developer settings, exchange it for a token, and the REST API handles statuses, follows and search. Because the whole platform is open source and federated, posting to it costs nothing and can point at an instance you run yourself.
If you only do one thing today, make it this one.

sections.heading: Bluesky At Protocol
paragraphs: First, the thing that actually matters: Bluesky runs on the open AT Protocol, whose public API is free — an account plus an app password is all a bot needs to post.

So what does that look like when you're actually doing it? createSession returns an access token, and app.bsky.feed.post publishes a post. No middleman, no paid 'basic tier' for your own account's posting, and the protocol is openly specified so the implementation is boring in the best way.
If you only do one thing today, make it this one.

sections.heading: Choose boring technology first
paragraphs: Skip the fluff and start here: The best infrastructure for a side project is the least surprising kind: static files, a public repo, a free CDN in front of it.

So what does that look like when you're actually doing it? Every exotic dependency is a future tax. If a free, open-source tool can serve the job, pick the one with the longest track record and the biggest community, and save the interesting experiments for the parts users actually touch.
Keep it this simple and you'll be ahead of most tutorials out there.
